headlines.title: San Francisco firefighters help battle Lucas Fire
headlines.description: More than a dozen San Francisco firefighters were deployed to help battle the Lucas Fire Saturday, according to the fire department. Authorities said 13 firefighters, a battalion chief and four type six wildland engines were deployed to the Lucas Fire. According to Cal Fire, the Lucas Fire has scorched 3,846 acres and is 15% contained. The blaze was reported on Thursday morning and prompted evacuations in Lake and Mendocino counties. The areas MNF-E016, MNF-E018, MNF-E019, UPP-E023, UPP-E025, UPP-E026, UPP-E027 and UPP-E030 in Lake County, along with the MEN-2POT08-B area in Mendocino County are under evacuation orders, according to Cal Fire. In Lake County, the areas MNF-E012, MNF-E013, MNF-E015, MNF-E017, MNF-E021, UPP-E028, UPP-E031, UPP-E032, UPP-E035 and UPP-E038, along with the Mendocino County areas MEN-2POT08-A and MEN-2UKV28 are under evacuation warning, Cal Fire said. An official evacuation shelter staffed by the American Red Cross Northern California Chapter opened at 6 p.m. Friday at Lake County Fairgrounds – Fritch Hall, located at 401 Martin Street in Lakeport, officials said. Evacuees may enter the fairgrounds through the C Street gate or the main gate off Martin Street, and parking is available behind Fritch Hall, the Lake County Sheriff’s Office said.

headlines.title: 3.4 magnitude earthquake shakes Contra Costa County
headlines.description: A 3.4 magnitude earthquake struck near Brentwood early Saturday morning, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 12:25 a.m. and was centered 6.9 miles east-northeast of Blackhawk and 7.0 miles southwest of Brentwood , the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. headlines.title: Los Gatos High community remembers and honors Flight 93 heroes
headlines.description: On Friday, Los Gatos High remembered two graduates who were on United Airlines Flight 93, the flight bound for San Francisco that crashed into an open field in Pennsylvania. Todd Beamer and Mark Bingham were among the passengers who came up with a plan to storm the cockpit and overtake the hijackers. A military flyover before the Los Gatos High School football game honored Beamer, Bingham and those who lost their lives on 9/11. Todd Beamer was a baseball player, and Mark Bingham was a star on the rugby pitch. Both were just a class apart. More than a decade after graduation they found themselves on the very same flight that fateful day, United Airlines Flight 93- Newark to SFO. Together they hatched a plan with other passengers to retake the plane from the hijackers. Beamer is credited with the rallying cry “let’s roll” as he and Bingham and the others made the ultimate sacrifice. Congressman Sam Liccardo spoke before the game tonight along with Los Gatos-Saratoga Union High School Superintendent Heath Rocha, who said 9/11 isn’t just part of the nation’s story but also a part of Los Gatos High School’s story. “This broke the heart of every American, on Sept. 11, particularly for folks here at home, it gave us something to hold onto, that we had some connection to those who rose above that moment of horror and terror, to demonstrate the best of America,” Liccardo said. “We want to carry on their story, and the takeaway is service over self. On that day, Todd and Mark knew they were giving their lives up in order to save thousands,” Rocha said. Now, a plaque sits at the front of Los Gatos High as a way for the community to honor Todd Beamer and Mark Bingham and a chance for the next generation to learn about their courage.

headlines.title: San Francisco honors the bravery of flight attendant Betty Ong during 9/11
headlines.description: On Friday, the community in San Francisco’s Chinatown honored Betty Ong, the flight attendant who made the first call reporting the hijacking of American Airlines Flight 11. Twenty-five years later, the community gathered to remember the courage she showed that day with a tribute at the Chinatown Night Market. They played a song honoring Ong. “She’s our hero who stood up and was the first call to report the hijackers,” Rev. Norman Fong, a longtime friend of Ong family, said. Ong grew up in Chinatown and later became a flight attendant. On Sept. 11, she made the first call alerting authorities to the hijacking. She remained on the phone for 23 minutes, calmly relaying what was happening on board before the plane crashed into the North Tower. Because of her call, all other planes got grounded. 23 years later, her courage still resonates with those celebrating her legacy. Ong’s brother Harry joined the tribute, thanking organizers for honoring his sister. “It still hurts you almost die 25 times. Every year yet you yourself want to forget 9/11, don’t ever forget, we just live with it,” Harry Ong told NBC Bay Area’s Jessica Aguirre. Ong’s legacy is a reminder that in a moment of crisis, ordinary people can do extraordinary things.

headlines.title: San Jose police officer fired for misusing Flock camera data, chief says
headlines.description: A San Jose police officer has been fired after being accused of accessing the department’s network of Flock license plate reading cameras for personal use, San Jose police Chief Paul Joseph said Friday. The controversial cameras have been under fire for months with many privacy groups saying the risk of abuse outweighs the benefit of the cameras for crime fighting. “This is a betrayal of the public trust — plain and simple,” Joseph said. “There’s no other way to put it.” The Automated License Plate Readers, or ALPRs, are a big part of police operations, which makes the violation by the police officer significant and an embarrassment to the department. Redwood City Aug 27 Palo Alto Aug 21 Brentwood Aug 17 SJPD said the cameras have been important tools in fighting crime. Police recently used them to track down an exceptionally dangerous armed robbery suspect. Officers managed to track the suspect even after he switched license plates. Critics of the cameras have repeatedly raised red flags, saying they can and have been misused by officers for personal or illegal reasons. San Jose leaders have tried to reassure critics and created safeguards. But on Friday the chief acknowledged the officers in the investigation is accused of accessing Flock camera data on his personal phone to help a family member last spring. “The officer accessed license plate reader data and provided that to a suspect in a domestic violence situation, which enabled that suspect to locate a victim,” Joseph said. “When we learned about this, we immediately placed this officer on administrative leave. We launched a criminal investigation into his conduct. We referred that investigation to the district attorney‘s office and we ultimately terminated that police officer.” Joseph said since learning about the incident, he has made changes to the policy to ensure the data cannot be accessed on a personal device. “I was furious that an officer would betray the public trust in that manner,” Joseph said. “That he would not understand how serious of a violation this is.” Immigrants rights group Services, Immigrant Rights And Education Network, or SIREN, is not satisfied with the fallout and said the cameras amount to mass surveillance and should be turned off. “Mass surveillance is not public safety and these cameras are only creating new threats,” said Kimberly Woo, a SIREN community organizers. “It goes way beyond just one officer and one vendor and one company because overwhelming evidence has shown across the country local agencies and ALPR vendors have grossly mishandled and abused our data.”

headlines.title: Students at Captain Jason Dahl Elementary in San Jose honor Flight 93 victims
headlines.description: September 11 for many is a moment to reflect and honor the victims of one of America’s darkest days. But at a San Jose elementary school bearing the name of one of those victims, Friday’s 9/11 memorial is not only about reflecting, but creating a more hopeful future. None of the current children attending Captain Jason Dahl Elementary was alive during 9/11, but nobody forgets the day on campus. San Francisco Sep 11 Los Gatos Sep 11 9/11 Sep 11 United Flight 93 crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania after passengers charged the hijackers on 9/11. The plane was headed to San Francisco International Airport and it is believed the hijackers intended to crash it into the U.S. Capitol. The pilot on that flight was Capt. Jason M. Dahl “When he was a student, he really dreamed of being a pilot,” Michelle Quilantang said of Dahl. Quilantang is the principal of Captain Jason Dahl Elementary in San Jose’s Seven Trees neighborhood. The campus is where Dahl went to school as a child, when it was known as Hillsdale Elementary. The school today bears Dahl’s name and a tribute to him adorns the main office. Every day at the campus is Capt. Jason M. Dahl day. And on the 25th anniversary of that tragic day, the lesson plan changes for the entire school. In a first grade class, students wrote thank you letters to their heroes. Among the heroes students wrote letters to were firefighters, police officers, teachers, and even Capt. Dahl. Students in a third-grade class used the word “patriot” to write synonyms with each letter — words like “protect” and “thankful.” Meanwhile, fourth graders took a deeper dive into 9/11. “Even though it was 25 years ago, we are still finding ways to make sure the legacy of September 11 and Capt. Dahl continues to live on for our students,” Quilantang said. “And that they ultimately do their best to be positive students in our school community.” Each student also had a second assignment to draw or write a good deed they promised to perform for someone else in memory of Dahl. The American flag at the campus on Friday was also flown at half-staff in memory of Dahl, an American hero whose memory now inspires a new generation to create a better world.

headlines.title: ‘A very devastating impact': Union City community honors Flight 93 victims
headlines.description: On Friday, the community in Union City gathered to honor the brave women and men on United Airlines Flight 93 that fought back against the hijackers during 9/11. There were 40 people on Flight 93, including 33 passengers and seven crew members; all of them fought back against the hijackers and sacrificed their lives to keep Flight 93 from reaching the hijackers’ target on Sept. 11, 2001. The plane ended up crashing into a field near Pennsylvania. “They knew that they were going to be used as a weapon of mass destruction and they chose to die rather than let that happen,” Union City Flight 93 Memorial Founder Michael L. Emerson said. Retired Marine Michael Emerson brought his vision for a memorial to Union City in 2002. Five years later, it opened as the world’s first municipal 9/11 Memorial, a place he hopes will keep the memory of the heroes sacrifice alive for generations to come. Forty granite stones honor the 40 people who lost their lives on Flight 93. The mirrors on each granite stone represent the people who died, and the possibility that any anybody could have been there. “These stones, you have a mirror on the front which reflects how you would’ve acted. The stone side and back are unfinished, and it represents an unfinished life,” he said. Lt. Col Frank Jamerson was in high school at the time of the attacks. His mom’s twin sister Wanda Green was a flight attendant born and raised in Oakland. Green was on Flight 93. “It’s hard, but also the fact that they were the flight that fought back, there is a large sense of pride. It is one of the reasons I’m wearing the uniform today,” he said. “It was a very devastating impact.” 9/11 24 hours ago 9/11 Sep 11 Kris Black hasn’t missed a 9/11 ceremony since the memorial opened in 2007. A fellow flight attendant’s son was also on that plane. “It was scary. Actually, as it was happening, I was at the airport and we knew a plane was missing and no one knew it and that’s when we found out it was Flight 93,” he said. “We have to be here every year, especially as crew members, too.” Following the official ceremony, many others also passed by throughout the evening to pay their respects in a more private way, including those who felt a particularly deep connection to the passengers and crew of Flight 93. Some families also passed by to teach their children about 9/11. Carolyn Rapier lives in Union City but says she grew up in New Jersey and frequently takes the same flight that Flight 93 was scheduled to make. “I feel particularly connected to that flight, because it could have easily been me,” she said. Michael Barravechia is from New York and now lives in the Bay Area. He lost coworkers in the 9/11 attacks. Standing at the memorial moved him to tears. “I love New York. This whole memorial for Union City, they did a wonderful job. I’m glad they did this,” he said.

headlines.title: 9/11 25 years later: SFFD Chief Dean Crispen reflects on how that day changed his career
headlines.description: Nearly 3,000 people died on September 11, 2001, among them 343 firefighters and 71 police officers. First responders ran toward the World Trade Center towers, knowing it could be their last call. In the aftermath of the smoke and rubble, departments from across the nation dispatched to New York, including a team from San Francisco Fire Department. Jessica Aguirre met with Chief Dean Crispen to reflect how the work he did that day as a volunteer, lessons learned and the impact it made on his career. Shortly after the nation’s ground stop was lifted, eleven firefighters from San Francisco packed their gear and headed to ground zero as volunteers, unsure of what they’d be doing or what they’d find. At the time, Crispen was a young firefighter on the department’s rescue squad, training on disaster responses. “Several members of the FDNY knew we were coming. So we’re able to kind of tell us, you’re not going to believe what you’re going to see,” said Chief Crispen. And, when he did arrive in New York. “Mass devastation,” he says, “I think we all thought we’d see big parts of buildings. We thought we would see, you know, just larger elements of the building and really it was all pulverized. It was incinerated.” The SF crew worked at ground zero for 10 days. “We were actually using buckets to remove debris and trying to find bodies. We were given very clear instructions that if we found anybody, FDNY pulls them out,” said Crispen. The firefighters also stood as honor guards for funerals of their fallen New York City brothers. “Every once in a while we’re on the pile … you’d hear the order to stop and that would mean that they found somebody and then everybody would turn towards the area that the person was found and salute and FDNY would do their ceremonious removal of the body that was very very difficult to witness.” Since 9/11, some 400 firefighters, who like Chief Crispen, rushed to help at the pit, have also died from health complications brought on from responding to that day. A battered steel beam from the World Trade Center sits in the lobby of SF fire headquarters, a reminder of the heroes lost and the sacrifices Chief Crispen and others made on September 11, 2001, 25 years ago. Crispen says, “In San Francisco, we talk about earthquake a lot, and that event clearly put a punctuation mark on disaster preparedness for any department and that’s been the 100% number one issue in my administration.”
headlines.source: Jessica Aguirre, Christine Ni and Jeremy Carroll

headlines.title: Grandcolas honors late wife and passengers of Flight 93 to generation not born on 9/11
headlines.description: Jack Grandcolas flipped on the garden hose and began dousing a backyard full of flowers at his Monterey County home. It felt kind of like a metaphor — a guy who’s spent the last 25 years publicly and privately grieving the loss of his wife Lauren in the September 11th attacks — somehow finally learning to bloom again. “I’ve had a lot of collateral damage in the last 25 years I’ve had to clean up,” Grandcolas said leaning back in a lawn chair. “But I’m feeling better than I ever have and happier than I ever have.” Lauren Grandcolas died on Flight 93 when it crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania on September 11th 2001. Her husband Jack has spent the last 25 years talking about his wife and the bravery of the passengers aboard the plane who tried to thwart the hijackers. It’s a significant pronouncement from Grandcolas, whose pregnant wife Lauren Grandcolas boarded United Flight 93 in Newark, New Jersey on September 11, 2001 to return to the couple’s San Rafael home. She’d flown back east to attend her grandmother’s funeral and to announce to the family that after 10 years of trying, she was three months pregnant. As hijackers took over Flight 93, she called her husband to let him know. Because of the difference in time zones, Jack was still asleep when she left her message on the couple’s answering machine, saying in a composed voice there was a problem with the plane and that she loved him. San Francisco Sep 11 9/11 Sep 8 9/11 Sep 10 As passengers rose up to retake the plane from the hijackers, it crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Watching the coverage from his home that morning, Grandcolas pieced together bits and pieces of news until the horror hit him. “I dropped to the ground because I knew that was the flight Lauren was calling from,” Grandcolas said, reciting the details he’s told countless times over the last quarter-century. Jack Grandcolas sits in the backyard of his Monterey County home. Grandcolas’ pregnant wife Lauren Grandcolas died on Flight 93 when it crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania on September 11th, 2001. Over the decades, Grandcolas has been a ready voice for the victims of 9/11 — willing to sit in front of cameras and share the details of the worst day and period of his life. He was devoted to talking about the bravery of the passengers who banded together to try and thwart the hijackers. Beyond the cameras, Grandcolas suffered grief, depression, loss, guilt, rage — the entire emotional range of a survivor. “The journey’s been a rough one for many, many years,” Grandcolas allowed. “It’s through the constant living in Lauren’s memory that’s helped. It’s through meeting my new wife Sarah that’s helped. It’s through meeting mental health professionals that’s helped.” In recent years, Grandcolas has shared his stories with a new audience; the people who were not yet born on September 11, 2001. He speaks in school assemblies, gymnasiums, libraries, telling the story of the Flight 93 passengers and their brave actions in trying to retake the plane, likely scuttling further tragedy as the plane hurled toward the U.S. Capitol or another high profile target. “A lot of these kids don’t have any point of reference,” Grandcolas said. “I found that out and have been giving talks to students to instill some inspiration to some of the good things that happened, some of the bravery, some of the heroes.” Grandcolas laments that only 25 states require teaching of 9/11 in public schools. It’s national history on one hand— he reasons — but on the other, it holds lessons that go well beyond what happened that day. “I think I can share some way of navigating problems, trauma,” he said, “inspiring them with Lauren’s story or the story of Flight 93 or just giving them a proper education to what it’s like to be a normal citizen thrust into a very intense situation.” In that sense, he sees his role not unlike survivors of Pearl Harbor who put a face on the attack and passed its lessons along to future generations. “The questions I get from these kids are unlike any questions I’ve ever been asked,” Grandcolas said, “and primarily I think because they have no living recollection of that day.” For the 25th anniversary of 9/11, Grandcolas will head to Shanksville, Pennsylvania like he does most years, to attend a ceremony at the sprawling memorial built in the field where Flight 93 crashed. The memorial stretches across bucolic, peaceful countryside, that otherwise offers no hint of the cataclysmic violence that occurred there. “If you hadn’t known the story, you would think it’s just a peaceful, beautiful area,” Grandcolas. Perhaps it’s another fitting metaphor for Grandcolas, who has long projected the composed demeanor of a loving, devoted husband, obscuring the inner turmoil and suffering he’s long endured. Yet 25 years later, Grandcolas feels his public and private emotions are now aligned. He appeared in the documentary called The Heroism and Resilience of 9/11, and wrote a book about Lauren and the passengers of Flight 93 called Like a River to the Sea. He feels the joy of his marriage to his new wife, Sarah Hopkins. And his guardian angel Lauren is always on his shoulder. It seems there in his backyard full of flowers, Grandcolas has truly figured out how to bloom again. “I’m finally to a place where I’m happy again,” he said above the stream of cascading water.

headlines.title: 2 Oakland police officers indicted on federal conspiracy, fraud charges
headlines.description: Two Oakland police officers were indicted last month for allegedly conspiring with a federal aviation official to fraudulently obtain pilot certifications. Brandon Mart and David Mac, both Oakland Police Department Air Support Unit helicopter pilots, allegedly conspired with a Federal Aviation Administration inspector to obtain the certifications between July 2023 and March 2024, according to a federal grand jury indictment filed on Aug. 27. The FAA official, William Miller, was an aviation safety inspector in charge of performing “checkrides,” flights in which people seeking pilot certifications are tested for mastery of an aircraft by completing flight maneuvers like takeoffs, landings and emergency operations. Checkrides also consist of an oral test, during which a person must demonstrate knowledge of aviation regulations, aircraft systems and weather, among other things. “The conspiracy involved the submission of fraudulent documents related to at least four separate checkrides, and resulting in Mart receiving three fraudulent certifications and Mac receiving one fraudulent certificate,” according to the indictment. All three men are charged with conspiracy to defraud the FAA and FAA registration fraud, which carry a combined maximum of eight years in prison. Mart is also charged with obstruction of justice by falsifying records, which carries a 20-year maximum penalty. The trio of defendants entered not guilty pleas during an arraignment Thursday in front of Judge Peter Kang of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California in Oakland. Bail was set for each at $25,000 and none of the defendants are currently in custody, according to court records. Attorneys for the three men didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment Friday. OPD Chief James Beere said the department found out about the indictment on Thursday and the officers have been placed on administrative leave. “We take these allegations seriously and are cooperating with outside law enforcement agencies as they conduct their investigation,” Beere said in a video statement posted online. “When I became chief of police, I made it clear that anyone who commits a crime in our city will be held accountable, including members of the Oakland Police Department, who are entrusted with a level of authority and responsibility that few others are given,” Beere said. “When an officer violates that trust, it not only undermines the integrity of that individual, but it also erodes the confidence our community has in the entire profession.” Evan Mateer, the federal prosecutor in the case, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The indictment comes at a particularly bad time for OPD, which has been under federal oversight for 23 years following the “Oakland Riders” scandal, during which police officers routinely falsified police reports, planted evidence, beat suspects and abused people’s civil rights. However, in May, OPD seemed closer than ever to shedding federal oversight, having finally reached compliance with dozens of court-ordered reforms, according to a report filed by the department’s federal monitor. A judge could make a decision on the federal oversight matter at a hearing scheduled for Sept. 29.

headlines.title: High fuel prices hit Bay Area food bank
headlines.description: Some gas stations in California are now charging nearly $10 for a gallon of diesel. Those prices have hit a Bay Area food bank especially hard, as it relies on trucks to deliver food to the community. The U.S. Bureau of Labor put out its latest inflation report on Friday, showing that fuel prices have jumped 28% in the last year, taking airline fares and energy prices up with it. In the Bay Area, fuel prices have hit food banks like Second Harvest of Silicon Valley especially hard, since they rely on trucks powered by diesel to deliver food to the food banks and out to the community. They said their fuel costs are up 48% from this time in 2025. The food bank said it is now spending about $73,000 a month on diesel fuel.

headlines.title: Woman dies after hit-and-run crash in San Jose
headlines.description: A woman died following a hit-and-run crash in San Jose Thursday night, according to the police department. San Jose police said officers responded to a report of a hit-and-run crash involving a pedestrian in the area of Rigoletto Drive and South King Road at about 8:52 p.m. A preliminary investigation found that a man driving a 2018 Toyota Tundra was traveling westbound on Rigoletto Drive and making a left turn at South King Road when he struck a woman who was crossing King Road in a marked crosswalk, police said. The woman was taken to a local hospital, where she later died. Her identity will be released by the Santa Clara County Office of the Medical Examiner. Police said the driver fled the scene before officers arrived. Officers used automated license plate reader cameras with assistance from the department’s Real Time Intelligence Center to locate the vehicle and apprehend the driver in San Jose, according to police. The driver was later booked into the Santa Clara County Main Jail on suspicion of crimes related to vehicular manslaughter and hit-and-run. The crash marks San Jose’s 34th fatal collision and 34th traffic-related death of 2026. It is also the city’s 17th pedestrian death of the year. The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information is asked to contact to contact Detective White #4638 of the San José Police Department’s Traffic Investigations Unit at: 4638@sanjoseca.gov or 408-277-4654.
